items.summary: Computational biologists increasingly delegate substantial analyses to AI agents in long-horizon, multi-turn sessions, yet most benchmarks of agents' bioinformatics capabilities pose a single short task with a single-shot prompt. We present OmicsBench, a long-horizon, multi-turn bioinformatics benchmark for AI agents. Each of its 97 tasks links dependent subtasks into a directed acyclic graph, for 662 underlying subtasks in all. Each subtask is posed as one user turn and graded deterministically against an answer key, with optional in-context feedback on incorrect answers. Across 12 models on three harnesses, the slowest agent averages 3.6 hours per task, and no combination comes near saturating the benchmark, with mean scores of 0.43 to 0.57 out of a possible 1 without in-context feedback and 0.54 to 0.67 with it. Multi-turn evaluation also uncovers behavior that single-shot prompts cannot, as agents score lower on subtasks that depend on earlier subtasks, and in-context feedback helps agents recover some of that loss. Because deterministic scoring gives no qualitative account of how an agent failed, we also introduce an unsupervised failure mode discovery pipeline that describes, embeds, and clusters agents' failed attempts to surface emergent failure modes. Applied to OmicsBench, this pipeline exposes qualitative shortcomings in how agents carry out bioinformatics analyses, ranging from agents applying their own statistical filters in place of the specified ones to agents writing whole answers from memory.
items.title: OmicsBench: a long-horizon multi-turn benchmark of AI agents on research-study-scale bioinformatics

items.summary: Segment Anything Model 3 (SAM 3) is a foundation model for image and video segmentation that sets the state of the art in visual object tracking. Its tracker, inherited from SAM 2, stores information from past frames in a memory bank, managed by a simple First-In-First-Out rule, allowing temporal consistency in complex videos. Several recent methods improve SAM 2 with hand-crafted memory update rules, each targeting a specific failure mode, such as distractors, occlusions, or object motion. However, their gains transfer only partially to the stronger SAM 3 backbone. We instead present a more general, data-driven approach that frames memory control as a sequential decision-making task. SAM3RL is an extension of the SAM 3 tracker with a lightweight memory controller, trained by reinforcement learning, that decides which frames enter the memory bank in order to maximize tracking performance. SAM3RL sets a new state of the art on 10 of 12 tracking and video object segmentation benchmarks, outperforming all hand-crafted rules without any runtime overhead. The same approach applied to SAM 2 gives SAM2RL, which outperforms hand-crafted rules on 9 of the 12 benchmarks, showing the generality of our method across model generations.
items.title: SAM3RL: Memory Control via Reinforcement Learning for Visual Object Tracking

items.summary: Distilling vision-language features into 3D Gaussian Splatting yields a language map that can be queried with arbitrary text. In deployment, however, a small set of user-specified targets must be reliably located, which current distilled maps often miss, while open-vocabulary queryability for other words must remain intact. We propose a training-free, target-aware refinement of an already-distilled language map. Guided by a text-promptable segmenter, the visual embedding inside each detected target region is blended with the target text embedding, a convex combination whose coefficient sets the amount of injected prior, while non-target regions are left untouched. Injecting too much overwrites appearance cues and general queryability, so we seek, for each target, the smallest coefficient that still lets it win, and we obtain every coefficient in closed form, leaving no hyperparameters to tune. We further identify a failure mode of injection in language-goal localization. Text embeddings share a common component, and injecting them makes the standard cosine read-out query-agnostic, which a centering step in the read-out removes. Across three benchmarks, the refinement consistently improves open-vocabulary segmentation, roughly doubling the base mIoU on Replica, and localizes language goals more reliably than the base map. It also transfers as a plug-in to off-the-shelf field-based and object-level language maps and supports a real-world demonstration in which a legged robot navigates to natural-language goals. Project page and code: https://lab-of-ai-and-robotics.github.io/target-aware-langmap/
items.title: Training-Free Target-Aware Refinement of 3D Gaussian Language Map

items.summary: Agent memory benchmarks evaluate whether an agent's responses reflect correct knowledge, measuring downstream question-answering accuracy as a proxy for memory quality. We show this evaluation paradigm is incomplete: it conflates memory correctness with retrieval and generation quality, producing both false positives where correct responses mask broken memory and false negatives where incorrect responses blame correct memory for retrieval failures. We introduce FEB-30, a benchmark of 30 fact-evolution trajectories spanning 6 diagnostic categories and 3 difficulty levels, constructed via paradigm inversion: documents are generated from known fact trajectories, yielding deterministic ground truth without human annotation. Each trajectory defines how a fact should evolve across multi-author artifacts (documents, emails, conversations), enabling direct inspection of the memory store after each ingestion step. Applying FEB-30 to a representative memory system, we demonstrate that intrinsic and extrinsic evaluation diverge by an average of 16 percentage points, with 44% of trajectories exceeding meaningful divergence thresholds. Diagnostic decomposition reveals that the system correctly classifies memory operations (create, update, reinforce, supersede) only 20% of the time, a failure entirely invisible to extrinsic evaluation, and that failure modes differ systematically by category and difficulty. We release the benchmark, document generation pipeline, and scoring framework to support reproducible evaluation of agent memory systems.
items.title: Beyond Downstream QA: Rethinking How We Evaluate Agent Memory

items.summary: LLM system capabilities depend not only on model parameters but also on the executable harnesses that organize information acquisition, tool use, reasoning, and memory. Recursive harness evolution can automate their design, but how it can reliably discover generalizable systems from limited, noisy, and repeatedly reused feedback remains unclear. We study this question in agentic video understanding, where rich multimodal evidence and coupled mechanisms make harness optimization challenging. We first introduce VideoHarness-BRSI, a recursive self-improvement framework that evolves video harnesses around a frozen vision-language model. Analyzing over 4,000 evolved candidates, we find it competitive with hand-engineered systems but identify three interconnected failure modes: validation overfitting, search-budget dilution, and the early-experience trap. We trace all three to a common root: the same imperfect validation evidence drives both harness revisions and the proposer's search strategy. We therefore propose VideoHarness-SRSI, an evidence-governed framework in which every search decision rests on evidence that is transferable, sufficient, and gathered before the search commits. It restricts the proposer to content-free feedback, informs exploration with instrumented warm-up experiments, and develops mechanisms in isolated probe-race branches before factorial composition and joint refinement. Across four video understanding benchmarks, VideoHarness-SRSI improves the equally weighted mean held-out score by 6.2% relative to VideoHarness-BRSI and reduces the mean validation-test gap by 37.9%. Reliable harness evolution thus depends on how search is organized and informed, not only on how well it optimizes validation performance.
items.title: VideoHarness-SRSI: Structured Recursive Self-Improvement for Video Understanding Harness

items.summary: We present an algorithm that computes the structural signature and the mean time-to-failure (MTTF) of a monotone binary system at every one of its states, rather than only at the state in which all components work. It makes no assumption on the structure function and evaluates it exactly once per state, as many times as needed for the signature of the complete system alone, so computing the MTTF everywhere costs only a factor polynomial in the number of components over computing it once. As a by-product, it identifies all minimal path sets. We assume exchangeable component failure times whose survivor count is a continuous-time Markov chain. This setting admits simultaneous failures, as in the Lévy-frailty Marshall-Olkin, binomial failure rate and lethal-shock models, where the simplifications available for single failures do not apply. We use the per-state MTTF to define threshold repair policies. We show that the per-state signature is a strictly finer decision criterion than the MTTF: signature dominance at a common failure count implies MTTF dominance, but not conversely. Under the Lévy-frailty Marshall-Olkin model the MTTF is monotone in the state, which yields the long-run cost rate of every threshold policy in a single pass. Experiments on 22 benchmark networks with up to 30 components and 31 failure models show that the best MTTF-threshold policy has a median excess cost of 0.36% over the optimal state-based policy, and that it is never worse than the best policy that repairs after a fixed number of failures.
items.title: Per-State Signatures and Mean Time-to-Failure: An Algorithm for Systems With Simultaneous Failures

items.summary: Agents are increasingly interacting with other agents that act for different principals (people or organizations on whose behalf they work), such as a buyer's personal agent negotiating with an enterprise's seller agent. In such agent-to-agent (A2A) scenarios, each agent has its own environment and holds information and authority that the other cannot see. Moreover, the interests of each agent may be aligned (cooperative), partly aligned (mixed-motive), or opposed (competitive). Existing multi-agent system failure studies assume one orchestrator, shared workspace, or single principal. We ask how A2A systems fail when these assumptions are removed. We study more than 2,500 recorded runs of A2A systems built from different agent harnesses and models, spanning 488 scenarios across eight families (legal, CRM, security, commerce, etc.). From these traces, we derive $A^2$-Failures, a taxonomy of 20 A2A failure modes in four categories: (i) discovery and delegation, (ii) grounding and record consistency, (iii) verification, and (iv) conduct and fidelity. Three findings hold across every harness, model, and scenario studied: (1) discovery and interaction are driven by the phrasing of the task rather than the availability of peer agents; (2) no agent verifies a peer's factual claim on its own initiative, so an A2A system inherits the reliability of its least reliable participant unless the protocol or mechanism performs the check; and (3) the aggregate outcome score credits the agent completing the task while staying blind to the coordination, verification, and conduct failures beneath it, so A2A systems must be evaluated per agent, against each agent's own principal. We release the run logs behind the taxonomy at https://huggingface.co/datasets/a2a-salesforce/a2-failures.
items.title: Why Do Agent Teams Fail Across Boundaries? A Failure Taxonomy for Agent-to-Agent Systems with Private States

items.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents can self-evolve at test time by accumulating experience: retrieving relevant memories before acting and writing new lessons back afterwards. Yet most are single-level: trajectories, distilled workflows and reasoning items all land in one undifferentiated pool indexed by embedding similarity, with no typed abstraction hierarchy. They never forget or deduplicate, and are prone to negative transfer, where a superficially similar but directionally opposite experience is recalled and its concrete steps are copied verbatim, actively harming the agent. We introduce STRATA, a structured, outcome-grounded, self-maintaining memory that organizes experience into a three-layer graph of atomic skills and code snippets, task workflows and generalized meta-frameworks, connected by typed edges. STRATA maintains itself through five mechanisms sharing one similarity geometry: a multi-dimensional similarity that scores retrieval by operation and target; a typed reflector crystallizing procedures from successes and pitfalls from failures; community detection that induces meta-frameworks; pressure-triggered garbage collection with articulation-point protection; and contrast edges that flag confusable, direction-opposite experiences. Across four interactive benchmarks (AppWorld, WebArena, ALFWorld, ScienceWorld), two frozen backbones and seven baselines, STRATA attains the best average score while simultaneously using the lowest latency and fewest environment steps of any memory-augmented method, and 44% fewer lines of injected memory than the most context-hungry baseline. We isolate two failure modes of prior memories: single-level memory degrades sharply as the task set grows, and single-level concrete memories suffer catastrophic negative transfer, which contrast edges repair, lifting ScienceWorld from 78.7 to 96.7 within the same system.
items.title: STRATA: Self-Maintaining Structured Experience Graphs for Self-Evolving Language Agents

items.summary: AUTONOMOUS NANOROBOTIC NAVIGATION AND MISSION OBSERVABILITY AT THE LIMIT First-Generation Research Flagship 01 | NANO/MICRO ROBOTICS, POWER & MISSION ENDURANCE Feng Cheng-en (33) x Starli This research atlas asks a difficult engineering question: when low-Reynolds-number microfluidic flows, Brownian orientation noise, boundary adhesion, external field actuation and incomplete sensing all influence a micro/nanorobot, what would justify calling its behavior autonomous navigation rather than externally assisted motion? The volume treats navigation as an auditable, bounded mission instead of an attractive trajectory. It develops a five-layer program spanning stochastic hydrodynamics, instrument and actuation provenance, uncertainty-calibrated belief-state estimation, blinded microfluidic challenges and independent requalification. Thirty linked mathematical stations differentiate physical relations, information-theoretic functionals and proposed navigation utility measures, with assumptions, dimensions and possible falsifiers. Eighty-two research chapters each open with a core mathematical relation, followed by five independent single-page research sections. Two hundred detailed Research Gates describe decisive comparisons, confounding explanations, evidence requirements, failure conditions and successor handoff artifacts. Thirty-three provisional Phoenix Answer Embryos offer revisionable research prototypes rather than predetermined conclusions. The key comparator is an equal-budget experiment: fixed-field sequences, microscope-assisted manual control, externally tracked predictive control and candidate fused navigation are evaluated under matched total energy, information access, geometry, time, collision limits and recovery obligations. The manuscript emphasizes blind targets, flow reversal, sensor dropouts, wall adhesion, correlated observations, full-system power accounting, censored failures and post-mission retrieval. A mission arriving at its target but leaving an unrecovered device is not counted as a fully closed success. This work is a hypothesis-generating Research Atlas v1.0, not an experimental report or a validated medical technology. External magnetic, acoustic, optical and microscope infrastructure must be disclosed; no in-vivo or clinical competence is inferred from bench-top movement. Foundational DOI-linked literature provides context, not proof of the proposed integrated system. Every major claim is designed to be revised, rejected or reconstructed by a successor team using raw evidence and pre-registered falsification rules. PARENT RESEARCH DOI https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23046134 Original parent: NANO/MICRO ROBOTICS, POWER & MISSION ENDURANCE AT THE LIMIT. Parent-chapter lineage: Ch. 06-11 (navigation), 47-51 (estimation/control), 65 and 68 (benchmarking and transfer). The current child manuscript does not yet have an independent DOI; one would be assigned only upon actual repository deposit. Editorial release note: the manuscript prioritizes non-duplicative research content and independent testability over an artificial word-count target. It is suitable as a research architecture for additional scientific review, not a substitute for physical validation.

items.summary: Multi-agent systems are increasingly used to solve coding tasks by coordinating agents that share code and plans. These agents are often optimized with reinforcement learning (RL) using automated evaluators, but bypassing evaluation can earn reward without producing a genuine solution. Prior work has largely treated reward hacking as a single-agent failure. In this work, we show that a reward-hacking strategy elicited in one agent can propagate to others and affect system coordination. Across four open-weight backbones, coding RL elicits and amplifies reward hacking in two settings: explicit mechanism descriptions in the system prompt and mid-training that models upstream exposure to facts about the coding environment. Using post-RL agents from the mid-training setting as sources, we observe propagation through code and shared memory, and across roles through natural-language plans. Even agents based on small open-weight models induce reward hacking in stronger closed-weight targets. On hard tasks, propagation can intensify along a transmission chain after the original source leaves as the code acquires more persuasive justifications. We also theoretically analyze conditions under which reward hacking amplifies, persists, or decays across agent interactions. Beyond propagation, reward hacking can bias task routing toward reward-hacking agents and survive candidate aggregation. As potential mitigations, we evaluate code review by the coder or a separate verifier, both of which reduce delivered hacks. Together, these results establish reward hacking as a transmissible strategy whose effects extend beyond the agent in which it first emerges.
items.title: Reward Hacking as a Transmissible Strategy in Multi-Agent Coding Systems

items.summary: In the paper, we establish congruences for twisted Dirac indices and signatures on closed string manifolds by specializing the two-parameter modular forms of Liu and Wang to the tangent bundle. Fourier coefficient comparisons yield uniform congruences modulo $3$ in dimensions $4k$, $1\leq k\leq7$. Suitable parameter choices give explicit formulas involving only genuine twisting bundles in dimensions $8,12,16,20,24,$ and $28$, and recover the comparisons of Chen and Han in dimension $24$. The level-one Witten genus further strengthens selected Dirac congruences to moduli $729,27,27,$ and $9$ in dimensions $16,20,24,$ and $28$, respectively. The proofs use Fourier expansions in reduced $K$-theory and integer identities obtained by clearing powers of two from the denominators before reduction modulo $3$. We also construct non-string spin counterexamples in each of the six listed dimensions and identify the additional coefficient that obstructs extending the uniform argument to dimension $32$ without further information.
items.title: Mod 3 Congruence Families for twisted signatures of string manifolds in dimensions up to twenty-eight

items.summary: We consider the three-dimensional Prandtl boundary layer equations near a smooth structured solution (u_s, K u_s) with ∂z K ≡ 0. Under a monotone-or-degenerate profile assumption on u_s(·), we prove local well-posedness, continuous dependence, and a priori estimates in the critical Sobolev space X^s = H^s_γ(r) × H^s_γ(q) × H^s_γ(∇{x,y} q), where r = u − u_s and q = v − K u. Our proof does not assume smallness of the data, monotonicity of ∂_z u_s, or Gevrey regularity. We also establish a nonlinear norm-inflation result showing that the raw H^s topology on q alone is insufficient, and we identify the minimal tangential derivative of q required. Several stress tests, counterexamples, and open problems are discussed.
items.title: Sobolev Well-Posedness for Three-Dimensional Prandtl Boundary Layers Near Proportional Structures in a Critical Transverse Space

items.summary: This record provides the public, non-confidential analytical and reproducibility materials supporting the manuscript “When Does Seismic–Geotechnical Data Fusion Add Value? A Borehole-Aware Empirical-to-Synthetic Validation Framework for Urban Tunnelling.” The study develops and audits a borehole-aware empirical-to-synthetic framework for evaluating whether adding downhole seismic information provides defensible incremental value in predicting the Ménard pressuremeter modulus under held-out validation. The empirical benchmark comprises 41 support-matched pressuremeter–seismic records across 21 independent boreholes from the Isfahan Metro Line 2 investigation. The framework compares a reference model, a geotechnical/geological-depth baseline, a seismic-only branch, naive multimodal fusion, and a dependence-aware fusion branch using leave-one-borehole-out validation. The public release contains a de-identified 41-record benchmark dataset, final manuscript Figure 1–5 assets, the current Supplementary Material and Supplementary Figure S1, released derived analytical outputs, provenance and reproducibility documentation, reproducibility and repository-audit scripts, computational-environment specifications, and SHA-256 integrity information. The de-identified dataset replaces source borehole identifiers with pseudonymous identifiers and excludes borehole coordinates and other spatially identifying source information. The underlying Isfahan Metro Line 2 geotechnical, geophysical, and pressuremeter source records are controlled by the Isfahan Urban Railway Organization and are not publicly redistributable. Original source workbooks, proprietary project documents, spatially identifying information, and other restricted source-derived materials are intentionally excluded from this public archive. Permission was obtained to use and publish the de-identified, non-confidential data extracted from the project report and the derived analytical information included in this release. The public code component provides scripts for reproducing the released manuscript-level benchmark metrics and verifying the integrity and consistency of the deposited files. These scripts do not contain the restricted original project records or proprietary source-data processing materials. The archive is intended to support transparent audit and reproducibility of the released derived analyses while preserving the access restrictions applying to the underlying project data.
items.title: When Does Seismic–Geotechnical Data Fusion Add Value? — Project 06 Data and Reproducibility Package

items.summary: Self-contained computational materials accompanying "Verifiable approval-release decisions for construction project management: A provenance-aware contract and automated evidence" by Ahmad Baghdadi. Version 4.0.0 includes source code, complete generated inputs and results, schemas, exact witnesses, a de-identified calendar encoding, benchmark records and SHA-256 checksums. This version adds 83 conventional priority-list levelling comparisons under identical constraints: 72 tied peaks and 11 one-gate improvements, with sufficient exact certificates for all 83. A complete two-plan PROV-O example passes the domain and provenance SHACL profiles and preserves every decision field after RDF exchange. The suite comprises 145 automated tests. Earlier computational evidence includes generated extraction, 360 controlled record comparisons, exact wave bounds, nine calendar scenarios and 80 saved benchmark plans with renewed arithmetic audit. S14 preparation includes blank independent-annotation and approval registers plus a precision/recall evaluator with explicit denominators. No native baseline or independent annotations are available; field validation has not been executed. Case A remains historical aggregates only. Calendar B is a prior encoding with assumed review windows. Supplementary Table S1 identifies the deposited components and the supplement consolidates the evidence limits.
items.title: Reproducibility materials for verifiable approval-release decisions in construction project management

items.summary: This data and code release accompanies “Output rules and corpus preparation shape retrieval evaluation in a cross-language legal information audit”. Version 3.0 brings together the current rule experiment, internal task benchmark, legal-version evidence and selected research exports from the published version 2.1 baseline. The collection contains 39 Peruvian legal-information records. The output-rule component applies eight combinations of no-match handling, document-support filtering and tie ordering to frozen scores for 32 retained queries and 58 designated-target exposures per language path. It includes 6,912 query-level results, 216 aggregate summaries and a 5,000-replicate shared-order negative control. The internal benchmark contains twelve tasks in six clusters, two formulations per task, 468 provisional content grades, the two returned coding sets, four retrieval configurations and corpus-repair comparisons. Current sensitivity files evaluate existing grade sets, all 27 assignments to three unknown returned grades and RETA-family aggregation. Preparation and judgment roles, prior-output exposure and missing values are retained. Content support is evaluated separately from temporal applicability. The legal-evidence component supplies dated official-source locators, checksums and version findings. The archive includes current Figures 1–3, source data, plotting code, component data dictionaries, a result/file map, portable standard-library recalculation code and a SHA-256 manifest. Exported score/rank aggregation and deterministic sensitivity checks have been reproduced. Fresh extraction and scoring require the exact source carriers, indexed text and pinned model resources documented in the manifests. Original legal PDFs, full-text/OCR caches, source-page images and model weights are not redistributed. Project-created data and documentation retain the existing CC BY 4.0 licence; project-created code retains the MIT licence. Third-party source materials remain subject to their respective access and reuse conditions. The preceding published baseline is identified by DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23094356, and the version series by DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23094355.
items.title: CLIQ-R: Data and code for cross-language legal retrieval evaluation in Peru

items.summary: Semiconductor spin qubits offer a promising route to compact and scalable quantum computers, combining long coherence times in isotopically purified silicon with compatibility with semiconductor manufacturing. Beyond computational speedup, their energy efficiency is an important consideration for future large-scale systems. We evaluate the power and energy requirements of a Loss-DiVincenzo spin-qubit quantum computer by analyzing the Quantum Fourier Transform (QFT) and benchmarking it against the classical Fast Fourier Transform (FFT). We develop a detailed energy budget, identifying cryogenic cooling as the dominant baseline contribution before quantum error correction (QEC). The comparison between the QFT and the classical FFT reveals that, for any quantum workload operating under a polynomially bounded sampling regime, the crossover in energy consumption occurs at smaller problem sizes than the crossover in execution time. Thus, quantum computing can become energetically competitive before achieving a speedup in execution time. We then incorporate surface-code QEC and analyze the energy costs of QEC cycles, gate synthesis, and decoding. At scale, instrumentation and decoding become dominant contributions, while cryogenic cooling imposes a constraint on scalability. We show that optimizing the control-signal demultiplexing ratio can reduce the overall energy cost by approximately two orders of magnitude. For a system with about one million physical qubits, we estimate a power consumption of approximately 100 kW, at least one order of magnitude below that of today's highest-performance classical computing systems.
items.title: Energetics of Fault-Tolerant Spin-Qubit Quantum Computation

items.summary: This replication package contains the experimental artifacts, anonymized empirical benchmark dataset (N = 5,000 paired student-opportunity records), statistical verification scripts, database definitions, and microservices source code for the research paper: "Hybrid Vector-Temporal Matching for Student Freelance Placement: An Empirical Study of Database-Level Vector Offloading" Targeted for Information and Software Technology (IST, Elsevier). Package Contents: data/: Anonymized benchmark dataset (students_data_tesis_final.csv) featuring 168-hour weekly availability matrices and raw ablation output. benchmarks/: Automated Python scripts for Stratified 5-fold cross-validation ablation (C1 to C4), Wilcoxon Signed-Rank hypothesis testing, Cliff's Delta effect size calculation, and bootstrap confidence intervals. database/: PostgreSQL 16 schema and stored procedure definitions for HNSW Approximate Nearest Neighbor vector search (pgvector) and dynamic schedule intersection. turborepo-src/: Clean source code of the decoupled microservices monorepo (API Gateway, Matching Service, ML Engine, and shared Protocol Buffers). System Requirements: Python 3.10+ with NumPy, SciPy, Pandas, Scikit-Learn, and NLTK. Node.js v20+ / pnpm v9+ and Docker Engine for microservice orchestration.
items.title: Replication Package: Hybrid Vector-Temporal Matching for Student Freelance Placement

items.summary: This Zenodo record is a permanently preserved version of a comment on a PREreview. You can view the complete PREreview and comments at https://prereview.org/reviews/22745390 . Thank you, Evgenii, for the detailed and constructive PREreview. Your comments led us to substantially strengthen both the experimental design and the interpretation of the results. We have now released a revised version of the manuscript that addresses the main points raised in the review. The revision includes: A 30-seed robustness analysis rather than relying on a single simulation seed A correlation sweep for estimator errors from ρ = 0 to 0.8 Regression-fitted and test-set oracle aggregation baselines Shared-noise experiments for the model–collective calibration signal, reported with ROC-AUC and lift Explicit specification of the four-Wave rolling calibration window, software versions, and PCG64 RNG Portfolio scaling to 100 Feature Blocks using an exact binary MILP reference An explicit separation between budget-constrained portfolio selection and ODP's native dependency-aware sequencing role An exact and scaling benchmark for ODP sequencing under prerequisite constraints An explicit competing-interest disclosure A public reproducibility package containing the simulation code, deterministic seeds, generated data, analysis scripts, and validation material. One particularly useful outcome of the revision was that the stronger experiments narrowed some of our original claims. For example, inverse-MSE aggregation performs very strongly when estimator errors are independent, but its advantage collapses under strong shared error. We also found that ODP distance is not the strongest heuristic for budget-constrained portfolio selection, while it performs very differently in its native sequencing role, where ERS/BVS is exactly optimal for the declared objective without dependencies and remains close to the exact optimum under the tested prerequisite constraints. Revised manuscript: https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.10648 Reproducibility package: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23261325 Thank you again for the review. It improved the paper. Competing interests I am a co-author of the manuscript discussed in this PREreview and a contributor to the D-POAF framework evaluated in the study. I am also affiliated with Inovionix, which develops software implementing D-POAF concepts.
items.title: Comment on a PREreview of "Governed Human-AI Prioritization Under Uncertainty: Adaptive Estimation and Dependency-Constrained Portfolio Selection"

items.summary: Multi-head latent attention (MLA) compresses the content of a key-value cache into a shared latent per token, making low-bit storage attractive for long-context inference. At two bits, errors in this representation perturb both attention matching and value readout, with effects that depend on error direction and reconstruction scale. We introduce RoLaQ (Rotation-calibrated Latent Quantization), an offline method for joint rotation and range calibration. RoLaQ refines a shared rotation within subspaces defined by the frozen key and value projections, and jointly learns quantization ranges whose thresholds and reconstruction gains are coupled to control the shared signal's response. Prediction matching and attention-output supervision guide calibration with model weights frozen. Across three MLA models and six benchmarks, RoLaQ achieves the highest average accuracy among the compared 2-bit methods both without and with token protection. On DeepSeek-V2-Lite, an SGLang implementation provides 3.96 times the BF16 KV capacity under the same memory budget and 2.51 times its decode throughput with 256K input tokens.
items.title: RoLaQ: Joint Rotation and Range Calibration for 2-Bit KV Caches in Multi-Head Latent Attention

items.summary: Multi-agent collaboration has emerged as a critical paradigm for tackling complex, long-horizon tasks; however, while coordination protocols continue to advance, systemic failures at the inter-agent collaboration interface remain a pervasive bottleneck. In collaborative workflows, systems frequently suffer from \emph{broken handoffs}---where critical task context is omitted, misrouted, or ignored despite each agent emitting locally plausible responses. To address this challenge, we present \method, a verifiable runtime control framework that treats handoff repair as selective intervention over explicit dependency graphs. Central to \method is an integrated fault-attribution and calibration pipeline, \dataset, which decouples execution dependencies and injects counterfactual handoff perturbations to provide empirical supervision for runtime intervention. Leveraging this diagnostic foundation, \method dynamically compiles observable interaction traces into a provenance graph to pinpoint unresolved dependencies, without accessing private agent states. It then evaluates candidate repairs through an empirical gate that weighs expected gains against disruption risks, and executes repairs only when formal local postconditions hold. Extensive evaluations across demanding benchmarks demonstrate that \method boosts task success by up to 12.3 absolute percentage points on SILO-BENCH and 11.1 on TeamBench. Across both backbones, \method maintains strict cost-effectiveness, adding as little as 2.0\% marginal token overhead. Furthermore, on 562 handoff-relevant traces from the MAST benchmark, \method achieves 69.8\% F1 in a single pass, establishing a reliable operational boundary for verifiable coordination repair.
items.title: BRIDGE: Selective Boundary Repair with Dependency Graph Evidence in Multi-Agent Systems

items.summary: Few-shot adaptation often relies on an encoder's final global representation, leaving complementary information in intermediate layers underused. Combining these features is challenging because their dimensions can differ and their usefulness varies across tasks. We propose LAMP, Layerwise Adaptive Mixing of Predictors, a training-free framework that combines global and regional information from multiple encoder layers. A single forward pass per view supplies all descriptors. Global and support-calibrated regional kernel predictors independently fit the same label residuals. Labeled validation data select their mixture in class-score space, preserving native feature dimensions without learned projections. LAMP-F further adapts text-anchored class prototypes, using a cached response to update the fixed-kernel residual predictions exactly. Experiments cover eleven datasets and ViT and ResNet backbones. LAMP achieves state-of-the-art mean accuracy among the compared published training-free ResNet-50 methods at 4, 8, and 16 shots, reaching 78.73% at 16 shots. Averaged across five support budgets, LAMP improves over a paired global-feature-only baseline by 1.14 and 1.59 percentage points on ViT-B/16 and ResNet-50; LAMP-F raises these gains to 1.96 and 2.54 points. LAMP-F reaches 16-shot accuracies of 83.57% and 79.10%, respectively. Controlled experiments identify multi-layer integration as the main source of improvement and examine pooling, calibration, validation labels, and computational cost. These findings show that combining layer-specific predictions can exploit complementary features from frozen encoders to improve few-shot classification.
items.title: LAMP: Layerwise Adaptive Mixing of Predictors for Training-Free Few-Shot Vision-Language Adaptation

items.summary: Level-2 (restricted) archive, version 1.0.1, of the replication package of the article Auditing successor selection in software repository mining: Evidence from filtering AI-attributed commits (H. Jeong, Hanyang University ERICA; manuscript under review). The public Level-1 archive with the programs, tests and aggregate results is https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23226958 (all versions; version 1.0.3, cited in the manuscript: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23430269). Changes in 1.0.1: two files with the per-identity counts of the exploratory published-measure analysis (file-based churn, cohort B; Supplementary Section S13 of the article) were added, re-keyed like the other cohort-B files; every file of version 1.0.0 is unchanged. The files are per-unit derived counts of the 3,687 cohort-A accounts and the cohort-B identities, with random identifiers (marker dates reduced to the month; no account names, e-mail addresses, repository names, commit SHAs or commit times). Placed by python3 reproduce.py --level2 <folder> of the Level-1 package (version 1.0.3), they recompute the registered aggregates and the exploratory aggregates that do not require the raw commit logs, including rates, transitions, paired contrasts, random-exclusion benchmarks and bootstrap intervals; on Python 3.10.12 with numpy 2.2.6 (Linux, aarch64) and on Python 3.13.16 with numpy 2.5.3 (Linux, x86_64) every regenerated result agreed with the reported one (numerical values within 1e-9, text files identical apart from line endings). Access is restricted because cohort-B rows keep the positions of their repositories in the public sampling order, which the registered repository-cluster bootstrap needs. Access is granted to researchers who state their name, affiliation and purpose and who agree to use the files only to verify, reproduce or extend the analyses of the article, not to redistribute the files or per-unit derivatives, not to attempt any re-identification or linkage to public commit histories or accounts, to store the files securely and delete them when the work is complete, and to cite the article and both archives (ACCESS.md). Reviewers of the article receive an access link through the editor.
items.title: Replication package (Level 2, restricted) for "Auditing successor selection in software repository mining: Evidence from filtering AI-attributed commits"

items.summary: This repository contains the curated research inputs, analysis code, and reference outputs supporting the study “Supplier identity can reverse estimates of global irrigation savings.” The study examines whether estimates of global irrigation savings depend on which suppliers reduce production, even when displacement quantities are held fixed within each market. It combines crop production, trade, and water-use data with constrained allocation models, historical production-contraction benchmarks, alternative water accounts, and conditional future scenarios for 2050 and 2100. Repository contents 01_Research_Inputs.xlsx — Curated source observations, geographic and crop identifiers, variable definitions, and source citations. 02_Research_Data.sqlite — Larger input datasets, archived analytical outputs, numerical checks, optional derived checkpoints, and an index linking the release to the associated manuscript and supplementary material. Source inputs and computed outputs are explicitly distinguished. 03_Analysis.py — Consolidated Python code containing the analytical modules, dependency specifications, input verification, and reproduction workflow. 04_Readme.txt — Documentation of data provenance, units, assumptions, reproduction instructions, licensing, and file checksums. The release corresponds to six main-text figures, 16 supplementary figures, and 24 supplementary tables. The exact associated manuscript and supplementary document versions are identified by their SHA-256 fingerprints. Data sources include ACEA, FAOSTAT, CWASI, GCAM scenario outputs, USGS irrigation water-use estimates, Kansas irrigation-technology replication data, and complementary water-account datasets. Source-specific citations and attribution requirements are retained in the documentation. Reproduction and validation The documented workflow uses Python 3.11. Separate dependency environments are specified where required. Installing dependencies requires internet access; the numerical analyses use the deposited inputs. Instructions cover the complete workflow and targeted reproduction checks. For version 1.0.1, file checksums, database integrity, and embedded assets were verified. The full-routing analysis was rerun from the deposited GCAM inputs for all 50 future configurations, reproducing the archived global water bounds and joint conservation outcomes within numerical tolerance. This targeted validation does not constitute a new execution of every stage of the study. Interpretation and reuse The modeled water bounds are conditional on specified technology responses, market quantities, supplier availability, production constraints, and water-use coefficients. They are not confidence intervals or globally identified causal effects of irrigation-technology adoption. Future configurations are conditional stress tests, not probabilistic forecasts. Original data compilations and documentation are released under CC BY 4.0, and original analysis code under the MIT License. Third-party inputs retain their source-specific licenses and attribution requirements, as documented in the README. Please cite this repository and the relevant original data sources when reusing the materials.
items.title: Data and code for "Supplier identity can reverse estimates of global irrigation savings"

items.summary: This repository contains the replication data and R code accompanying the study “From Periodic VAT Listings to Real-Time Reporting: Digital Reporting Requirements, Business Information Architecture and the EU VAT Compliance Gap”. The replication package combines European Commission VAT compliance gap data with a manually verified longitudinal coding of mandatory Digital Reporting Requirements across 26 European Union Member States over 2013–2023. The analytical panel contains 284 country-year observations. The policy coding harmonises periodic VAT listings and control statements, SAF-T and invoice-data reporting systems, and continuous or near-real-time transaction controls within a common information-governance framework. Alternative coding scenarios are retained to document uncertainty associated with implementation dates, phased rollouts and differences in reporting architecture. The accompanying R scripts reproduce the analytical dataset construction, descriptive statistics, two-way fixed-effects models, country-specific trend specifications, first-difference analysis, alternative treatment codings, architecture comparisons, panel diagnostics, staggered-adoption diagnostics and wild-cluster bootstrap inference reported in the study. No pre-computed analytical results are included in the repository. All derived results can be reproduced from the supplied input workbook and R scripts. The underlying VAT compliance gap data originate from the European Commission, Directorate-General for Taxation and Customs Union. The original DRR coding and its documentation were compiled by the authors from official European Commission and national tax-administration sources. The authors’ original data compilation and policy coding are made available under CC BY 4.0. The R replication code is released under the MIT License. Underlying third-party data remain subject to the terms of their original providers.
items.title: Replication Data and R Code for "From Periodic VAT Listings to Real-Time Reporting: Digital Reporting Requirements and the EU VAT Compliance Gap"

items.summary: Analysis code and computed evidence store for the manuscript "An exact recurrence test for acquisition-chain bounds in vehicle telemetry: the closed ECU surface yields nothing, and the one detection lies in the logger we built ourselves", submitted to Sensors and Actuators A: Physical. This deposit contains code and derived results only. The underlying telemetry is published separately under its own DOIs, which fetch_data.py downloads and checksum-verifies before analysis, so the published figures are reproducible from the public record. Study design: observational audit of already-deposited telemetry (seven recording sessions). No experimental control, no intervention, no independent replication, and no statistical power for population-level inference. Headlines formulated after measurement rather than pre-declared in config.json are labelled exploratory in the manuscript. Multiplicity: this deposit is one of 15 analyses drawn from the same corpus of seven sessions, one vehicle and one rider. No correction for multiple comparisons is applied across that family, so the family-wise error rate is not controlled. Repository commit of record: 37f7b2147b26
items.title: Reproducibility package (I-21): An exact recurrence test for acquisition-chain bounds in vehicle telemetry: the closed ECU surface yields nothing, and the one detection lies in the logger we built ourselves

items.summary: Long-term agents face growing storage demands as they accumulate experience. World models capture reusable regularities that can reduce the information stored for each experience. We formulate the problem of memory allocation conditioned on a world model and introduce MemoWM, a framework that uses shared predictions to compress retained information and reconstruct omitted content. Its task-aware allocation rule balances the expected impact of reconstruction errors against storage cost, retaining information with downstream value beyond the predictive prior. Across five long-term agent-memory benchmarks, MemoWM achieves 42.42\% average answer accuracy, exceeding the strongest baseline by 2.62 percentage points, while reducing average experience-specific storage by 53.9\% relative to MIRIX, the most storage-efficient baseline. Further analysis shows that stronger world models reduce per-experience storage at comparable task quality. Accounting for model parameters reveals a trade-off between shared model capacity and recurring storage costs, with the capacity that minimizes total storage increasing as more interactions are retained. Our code is available at https://github.com/Feld-maxiu/MemoWM.
items.title: MemoWM: How World Models Change What Agents Need to Remember

items.summary: We have presented a mathematically closed, comprehensive foundation for the C861 discrete spectral benchmark. By establishing the exact rank-two projector geometry, resolving Dirichlet sum cancellations, providing constructive proofs for linear B-spline KAN operator reproduction, and formalizing the Lyapunov convergence of Dense Associative Memory on spherical manifolds, this framework eliminates ambiguities in evaluating learned physical operators. Furthermore, the spectral interlacing analysis of the CN → PN structural homotopy equips the scientific machine learning community with a tool to distinguish authentic topological sensitivity from numerical discretization artifacts.
items.title: Exact Discrete Spectral Invariants as a Falsification Baseline for Learned Operator

items.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents can self-evolve at test time by accumulating experience: retrieving relevant memories before acting and writing new lessons back afterwards. Yet most are single-level: trajectories, distilled workflows and reasoning items all land in one undifferentiated pool indexed by embedding similarity, with no typed abstraction hierarchy. They never forget or deduplicate, and are prone to negative transfer, where a superficially similar but directionally opposite experience is recalled and its concrete steps are copied verbatim, actively harming the agent. We introduce STRATA, a structured, outcome-grounded, self-maintaining memory that organizes experience into a three-layer graph of atomic skills and code snippets, task workflows and generalized meta-frameworks, connected by typed edges. STRATA maintains itself through five mechanisms sharing one similarity geometry: a multi-dimensional similarity that scores retrieval by operation and target; a typed reflector crystallizing procedures from successes and pitfalls from failures; community detection that induces meta-frameworks; pressure-triggered garbage collection with articulation-point protection; and contrast edges that flag confusable, direction-opposite experiences. Across four interactive benchmarks (AppWorld, WebArena, ALFWorld, ScienceWorld), two frozen backbones and seven baselines, STRATA attains the best average score while simultaneously using the lowest latency and fewest environment steps of any memory-augmented method, and 44% fewer lines of injected memory than the most context-hungry baseline. We isolate two failure modes of prior memories: single-level memory degrades sharply as the task set grows, and single-level concrete memories suffer catastrophic negative transfer, which contrast edges repair, lifting ScienceWorld from 78.7 to 96.7 within the same system.
items.title: STRATA: Self-Maintaining Structured Experience Graphs for Self-Evolving Language Agents

items.summary: Long-horizon multi-agent collaboration requires memory that preserves both successful actions and the coordination structure underlying them. Existing memory systems support information sharing or procedural reuse, but often leave the evolution of shared procedures disconnected from the task dependencies and execution states of collaborating agents. This coupling also limits the direct transfer of procedural memory designed for individual agents to team settings. We propose Self-Evolving Procedural Memory (SEPM), a framework that uses task dependency graphs as a common representation for online coordination and procedural memory evolution. During execution, a lightweight shared blackboard records structured evidence alongside task dependencies, supporting the detection of goal, plan, and world-state divergence and evidence-based realignment. After execution, verified actions and dependencies are distilled into reusable procedures, while recurring failures inform warnings and constraints. The shared procedure pool evolves through creation, refinement, specialization, and retirement, guided by success and cost utility and constrained by evidence and safety requirements. Together, these mechanisms preserve the collaborative structure and applicability conditions needed to reuse experience across tasks. Evaluations on ALFWorld, WebArena, and OfficeBench under AutoGen and DyLAN show that SEPM achieves the highest task scores among the compared methods in all six benchmark settings. Under AutoGen, it improves task scores over the no-added-memory baseline by 29.85, 25.86, and 13.00 percentage points, respectively. The codebase is available at https://github.com/cookieApril/SEPM.
items.title: SEPM: Self-Evolving Procedural Memory Grounded in Task Graphs for Multi-Agent Collaboration

items.summary: Long-horizon robotic manipulation is often built by chaining independently trained skills. Although each skill can be reliable in isolation, performance degrades sharply when skills are chained: each downstream skill must start from the state its predecessor leaves behind rather than from its training distribution. We study this failure mode, Observation-Space Shift (OSS), and ask what causes these skill-seam failures. Using privileged simulator resets, we find that the dominant shift comes from displaced scene state (e.g., an open drawer or secondary objects left behind by earlier skills), not from the robot's joint configuration or the object the downstream skill manipulates. To test this diagnosis, we build a fully learned detect-restore-resume system: a task-progress monitor detects the stall, a learned policy restores the displaced scene components, and seam-robust fine-tuning lets the skill resume. It recovers the seam where every tested alternative fails, which we treat as evidence for the diagnosis rather than as a general-purpose method. On the BOSS-44 benchmark, the system improves full-chain success from 7.6% to 26.5%, a 3.5x improvement over the base policy and 51% of a privileged restoration oracle, whereas best-of-K resampling, a Diffusion Policy, and world-model baselines fail to recover from the evaluated seam states. On a real Franka arm running a fine-tuned $π_{0.5}$ policy, the same monitor is limited by exterior-camera observability, yet closing the loop still recovers some otherwise-terminal failures, motivating wrist and gripper sensing. These results suggest that some long-horizon composition failures are better addressed by restoring the scene before resuming the policy than by retrying from an off-support state.
items.title: Diagnosing and Recovering from Observation-Space Shift at Long-Horizon Skill Seams

items.summary: Persistent memory can improve personalization in LLM agents but can also induce sycophancy and cross-domain leakage. We distinguish two governance decisions: admission, which determines what recalled information enters the working context, and presentation, which determines how admitted information is expressed. We implement two inference-time designs without retraining: factor-compiled admission (FC), which assesses whole memory entries, and permission-semantic admission (PS), which decomposes entries into typed units; both translate adjudicated attributes into eligibility decisions via deterministic policies. We evaluate on a four-backbone development suite and an external benchmark with four tasks of 300 samples each. Relative to verbatim injection, FC and PS reduce pooled judge-assessed failure rates on the external benchmark by 6.7 and 8.8 percentage points (p = 2.7e-7 and 4.1e-12), and development-set cross-domain leakage falls by up to 29.5 percentage points. A query-conditioned gating baseline shows no significant change in objective-fact failure or pooled failure. Under matched admission budgets, PS outperforms random and relevance-based selection on external objective-fact judgment after Holm correction. Holding presentation fixed, tightening admission cuts cross-domain failure by a further 17.5 percentage points (p = 1.6e-4); in contrast, no comparison between two renderings of identical adjudicated outputs survives multiple-comparison correction. Both designs increase personalization failures, and PS misses the preregistered improvement and personalization-preservation criteria. These results support evaluating admission and presentation separately: selection quality provides task-specific safety gains, while preserving beneficial memory use remains unresolved.
items.title: What to Admit and How to Present: Governing Persistent Memory in LLM Agents

items.summary: Accurate simulation of rigid-body interactions is essential for predictive physical world models. Despite recent progress in modeling object dynamics, capturing how local contacts between surfaces shape object motion remains challenging. While end-to-end world models predict interactions across entire scenes or objects, in practice, rigid-body contact is inherently local, and only nearby surfaces can directly exchange contact forces. Motivated by this observation, we introduce Rigid-body Contact Reasoning (RiCo), which represents interactions between objects through sparse neighborhoods of contact surface points. RiCo combines each point's state with the relative geometry, motion, and physical properties of nearby surfaces, then reasons across the object's points to determine how these local contacts jointly affect its motion. By confining cross-object reasoning to nearby surfaces while propagating contact information within each rigid body, RiCo retains fine-grained interaction details without the cost of modeling every pair of scene points. Such properties enable RiCo a higher accuracy and contact fidelity. Experiments on MOVi-benchmark demonstrate that RiCo reduces 100-frame position and orientation errors by 31-35% and approximately 38%, respectively, compared with baselines. Moreover, RiCo achieves high contact fidelity, with ground-truth-relative penetration-time and mean-depth differences of 11.0% and 2.22 mm, respectively. RiCo further generalizes zero-shot from small-scale training scenarios to scenes containing 270 objects. Our real-world multi-ball collision experiments further provide preliminary evidence of sim-to-real transfer.
items.title: RiCo: Neural Simulation of Rigid-Body Interactions via Local Contact Reasoning

items.summary: Weight-space learning across architectures requires representations that respect parameter symmetries and scale to large networks. Existing equivariant tensor encoders require architecture-specific symmetry specifications, while neuron graphs make global attention costly. We introduce a typed graph organized around shared coordinate-permutation actions. Its nodes, called interfaces, represent coordinate spaces whose bound tensor axes must be permuted jointly; operation occurrences, called modules, form typed hyperedges. A compiler derives this graph from supported PyTorch models, with exact recovery of the permutation factors defined by its constraints. The Universal Weight Encoder (UWE) combines local equivariant updates to parameter features with global attention over invariant interface summaries. The small number of interfaces makes global attention practical, and a single encoder processes different supported architectures. UWE is competitive with architecture-specific state-of-the-art methods on established benchmarks. On a new zoo of 1,200 transformers spanning 100 architectures, it outperforms the evaluated baselines at ranking networks within unseen architectures, including architectures larger than those used for training, while using substantially less memory.
items.title: Interfaces and Modules: A Scalable Representation for Weight-Space Learning across Architectures

items.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents solve complex tasks by calling external tools over multiple turns. Recent work has proposed tool graph memory, which stores past experience as tool transitions to guide subsequent selection. However, it remains unclear whether this component consistently improves agents' tool use or undermines it. We evaluate tool graph memory on nine models and two benchmarks, finding that it seldom improves significantly over baselines, and that its gains, where present, cost over twice the LLM calls. The memory's guidance is often incorrect, and random or no guidance retains most of the gain, implying that the benefit stems from extra computation rather than the memory itself. Moreover, even with the correct next tool suggested, many failures remain, such as giving up without a tool call. Storing the same experience instead as textual insights outperforms tool graph memory with almost no extra LLM calls. This suggests that memory serves better as a soft prior than as a prescription of the next tool, leading to a more effective and generalizable solution.
items.title: Rethinking the Role of Tool Graph Memory in Multi-Turn Tool Use

items.summary: Key-value (KV) cache management has become a critical bottleneck for scaling Large Language Models (LLMs) to long-context scenarios due to linear memory growth. While recent eviction methods have moved beyond simple attention-score heuristics to incorporate value representations, they typically face a fundamental trade-off: the underlying optimization for minimizing output perturbation is an NP-hard combinatorial problem, leading to mathematically suboptimal heuristics or implementations that are difficult to kernelize. In this work, we propose DropKV, a simple principled eviction framework based on Decoupled Residual-Output Perturbation. By decoupling the joint eviction decision into independent per-token scoring, DropKV circumvents combinatorial intractability and admits a provable constant-factor approximation guarantee under a cone condition that we empirically verify on three long-context LLMs. To ensure practical viability, we provide a high-performance implementation using fused Triton kernels that avoid materializing the full attention matrix, delivering a 19.8x scoring-kernel speedup that translates to up to a 9.9% matched-batch end-to-end prefill speedup. Extensive evaluations on the RULER and LongBench benchmarks demonstrate that DropKV consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines at equivalent cache budgets, achieving the lowest inference latency among eviction methods while also remaining faster than the dynamic cache baseline.
items.title: DropKV: Decoupling Residual-Output Perturbation for Near-Optimal KV-Cache Eviction

items.summary: As Vision-Language Models (VLMs) advance, they are increasingly expected to perform spatiotemporal reasoning over motion, actions, and view changes beyond what the input images show. Video World Models (VWMs) provide a natural unified engine for visual imagination by generating task-relevant visual content as additional evidence. However, existing approaches typically invoke a VWM through fixed pipelines centered on a predefined form of visual imagination, such as novel-view synthesis. To support flexible visual imagination for diverse reasoning tasks, we introduce CoWorld Reasoner, an agentic framework that uses a VWM as a unified visual reasoning engine. Its Video World Model-Driven Harness exposes multiple visual operations through tools and uses skills to guide the VLM in deciding whether to imagine, selecting an operation, constructing a generation request, and interpreting the resulting visual evidence. We further introduce VLM-VWM Harness Co-Evolution, which jointly revises tools, skills, and execution code based on execution feedback while keeping both model weights fixed. Across seven benchmarks spanning spatial intelligence, temporal and causal reasoning, and perceptual reasoning, CoWorld Reasoner outperforms direct reasoning with the same VLM. The strongest variant improves on all seven benchmarks, including relative accuracy gains of 11.8% on MMSI and 13.0% on ERQA, and outperforms all five evolving baselines using the same backbone across five benchmarks.
items.title: CoWorld Reasoner: Agentic Multimodal Reasoning with the Evolving Video World Model-Driven Harness

items.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents for portfolio management learn from experience: they credit each experience in their memory with the outcome of the decisions that used it. In financial markets, however, this outcome mostly reflects the market move shared by all decisions on that date, so the credit tracks the market rather than the experience, and these agents often do worse than simply holding the equal-weight (1/$N$) portfolio. We ask how an agent can credit an experience with what it changes, and answer it by putting memory on trial: drafts of the same decision with and without an experience face the same market, so the outcome they share cancels in their difference. Our agent, MemTrial, drafts each decision with eight combinations of its retrieved experiences, chosen by a fractional factorial design, and credits each experience with its Banzhaf value, the average of these differences. As each date occurs once and each draft is a noisy LLM sample, these credits are noisy and may not hold on new dates. MemTrial therefore pools them across dates and similar experiences with a hierarchical Bayesian model, acts on them only after they have predicted unseen dates, and otherwise stays anchored at a conservative reference such as 1/$N$. On four benchmarks, MemTrial not only benefits from experiences that matter (the best of 15 methods on a semi-synthetic benchmark with known experience quality) but also limits its losses when its values do not hold (at most 2.2\% below 1/$N$ on PortBench and InvestorBench, against 15--38\% for the best experience-learning agent). Averaged over five settings, it improves the utility of the best experience-learning agent by 21.2\%, and with eight LLMs it beats every LLM-based baseline on InvestorBench.
items.title: MemTrial: Learning When to Trust Memory in LLM Portfolio Agents

items.summary: Recent advances in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) and 3D generation have expanded 3D understanding and synthesis. However, beyond visual fidelity, task-specific correctness grounded in 3D evidence remains a major challenge. We argue that building reliable 3D systems requires not only stronger generation and reasoning, but also verification feedback that identifies unmet requirements and explains their violations, allowing systems to reflect on and refine their outputs. Such feedback must integrate multi-view observations and distinguish genuine inconsistencies from projection-dependent appearances. We make three contributions. First, we introduce 3DVerifierBench, a benchmark spanning 10 tasks that evaluates decisions, rejection explanations, and responses to controlled changes in specifications and candidates. A human study reveals a 21.6 percentage-point gap between humans and the strongest tested model, GPT-6 Astra, while explanation-aware analysis exposes weaknesses in rejection reliability. Second, we analyze verification across fine-grained factual categories, exposing errors in values and target binding. We develop a scalable pipeline combining multi-view fact extraction, controlled 3D editing, and native annotations to produce 14,126 training examples with contradiction explanations and linked counterfactuals. Third, we examine how verification could support 3D generation through candidate selection and recursive refinement. In human-labeled sixteen-candidate pools, oracle selection improves complete factual success from 26.7% to 90.0%. In a separate eight-input study, human-guided recursive refinement satisfies all seven requirements for every input, compared with three under parallel Oracle@8. Together, our benchmark, analysis, and data pipeline establish a foundation for models to reflect on 3D content through reliable verification feedback.
items.title: Grounding Generative Verification in 3D Content

items.summary: Segment Anything Model 3 (SAM 3) is a foundation model for image and video segmentation that sets the state of the art in visual object tracking. Its tracker, inherited from SAM 2, stores information from past frames in a memory bank, managed by a simple First-In-First-Out rule, allowing temporal consistency in complex videos. Several recent methods improve SAM 2 with hand-crafted memory update rules, each targeting a specific failure mode, such as distractors, occlusions, or object motion. However, their gains transfer only partially to the stronger SAM 3 backbone. We instead present a more general, data-driven approach that frames memory control as a sequential decision-making task. SAM3RL is an extension of the SAM 3 tracker with a lightweight memory controller, trained by reinforcement learning, that decides which frames enter the memory bank in order to maximize tracking performance. SAM3RL sets a new state of the art on 10 of 12 tracking and video object segmentation benchmarks, outperforming all hand-crafted rules without any runtime overhead. The same approach applied to SAM 2 gives SAM2RL, which outperforms hand-crafted rules on 9 of the 12 benchmarks, showing the generality of our method across model generations.
items.title: SAM3RL: Memory Control via Reinforcement Learning for Visual Object Tracking

items.summary: EnCert is a compiler-level formal verification framework for checking Namespace-protected LLVM IR produced by the Zeno capability architecture. It decomposes post-transformation verification into two complementary stages: thoroughness verification, which checks that covered memory accesses use valid protected pointers with consistent Namespace size, lifetime, and replacement behavior, and functional-preservation verification, which uses normalization contracts and Alive2 to determine whether the protected program refines the original program for supported valid executions. The artifact includes the EnCert LLVM passes, evaluation scripts, benchmark inputs, controlled mutation infrastructure, and reference results used to reproduce the experiments on EnForge-protected MSET programs, including the detection of protection violations and functional corruptions reported in the paper.
items.title: EnCert

items.summary: Long-horizon embodied agents must maintain task-relevant information, coordinate heterogeneous robots, and adapt their decisions as execution unfolds. Existing benchmarks investigate dynamic task execution and embodied multi-agent coordination, but provide limited evaluation of their intersection. We introduce MAGMA-Bench, an architecture-agnostic benchmark for persistent task reasoning in dynamic multi-robot environments. MAGMA-Bench evaluates agents across increasing task horizons and controlled online perturbations, including execution failures, task interruptions, and mission updates, with scenarios requiring coordination across robots with heterogeneous capabilities. It uses a structured skill-level interface to separate task-level reasoning from perception and low-level control. We evaluate locally deployable open-weight planners, multi-agent state-tracking strategies, and frontier models. Even the strongest evaluated models fail on a substantial fraction of clean episodes, and their success rates decrease further under online perturbations. Supervised adaptation greatly improves a small model, but performance remains substantially lower on longer and multi-robot missions. We release the benchmark, 261,646 task-level training examples, and an architecture-agnostic expert-trace generation pipeline.
items.title: MAGMA-Bench: Evaluating Long-Horizon Embodied Agents under Dynamic Tasks and Execution Failures

items.summary: It is assumed that a natural way to improve the pedagogical quality of large language model tutors is to define a metric of instructional performance and fine-tune the model against it. To test this strategy, we designed a metric of pedagogical adaptivity that scores each instructional decision in a learning sequence against the conditions of the learning situation, which is the standard used for automated pedagogical scoring. We audited a frontier tutor across 2,000 learner scenarios, corrected its weakest cases by fine-tuning an open-weights proxy, and asked 31 trained educators to rate the pedagogical alignment of the outputs blind, before and after correction. The metric increased from +0.05 to +0.42 for the corrected cases, while the expert ratings decreased from 4.46 to 3.03, with the unmodified controls remaining unchanged and a base-proxy control ruling out the change of model. The tutor performed worse because any metric that scores decisions independently and averages them is maximized by repeating the single best decision, and the fine-tuned model collapsed to that exact optimum in every case, in and out of sample. Educators identified the repetition, which such metrics cannot represent, and preserving the learner's trajectory in the score reduced, but did not reverse, the metric's verdict. Weight analysis traced the correction to the model's output projection, where it had memorized its training strings rather than learned to adapt. We conclude that measurement validity does not imply optimization validity, and we derive design principles for benchmarks that assess or train AI-tutor instruction.
items.title: The learner who does not learn: when optimizing a pedagogical metric degrades LLM tutoring

items.summary: Multi-agent path finding (MAPF) solvers are evaluated on the schedules they produce, not on how well those schedules can be executed. Specifically, continuous-time optimal solvers can achieve even lower cost than their discrete counterparts by scheduling agents with near-zero temporal/spatial separation, and by exploiting graphs with higher connectedness; however, such schedules may prove hard to execute under a realistic controller. We integrate AOC-CBS, an anytime-optimal continuous-time MAPF solver, into a fleet coordination framework in which each agent tracks its timed path using model predictive control, and we evaluate the resulting system on congested MovingAI benchmark instances with 21 to 40 agents. Without intervention, only a fraction of the instances complete execution. We then apply T-robustness by adding a time-margin, i.e., a minimum temporal gap between agents at shared locations, as well as spatial inflation of the agent footprint. Increasing either margin raises execution success, for a relatively small increase in the schedule's sum-of-costs; it also improves how closely agents adhere to the schedule: when tracking each agent's position throughout execution and comparing it against the position it should occupy according to the schedule, the mean discrepancy falls significantly as the margin increases. In general, the two margins have different effects; temporal margin decreases deviation, giving the controller room to stay on schedule. Spatial margin affects deviation less and instead increases the clearance between agents, so that the same deviation no longer leads to a blocking stall. They are nonetheless substitutes rather than complements: spatial inflation is almost free in schedule cost, but its effect on execution success is small and does not compound with a temporal margin already in place.
items.title: The Cost of Executability: Temporal Margins for Continuous-Time Multi-Agent Path Finding under Closed-Loop Control

items.summary: Offline MARL increasingly relies on generative policies to model multimodal joint behavior, typically by distilling a centralized teacher into decentralized one-step actors under the CTDE. We identify a failure mode at the teacher training stage: standard flow-based teachers pair noise with replay targets independently, so nearby noise samples can be routed toward conflicting coordination modes. The teacher then produces samples between valid modes, and because the distillation loss regresses each local actor onto the conditional mean of the teacher's output given local input, this error is not absorbed but propagated to the student. To remove this teacher-side artifact, we propose Mode-Support Semi-Discrete Optimal Transport (MoSDOT), which summarizes multimodal replay into a finite mode support with prescribed capacities and uses conditional semi-discrete optimal transport to assign each noise sample to a single mode before teacher training. We additionally study a shared-randomness variant that uses a shared noise component at execution to expose the residual gap intrinsic to strict-product execution. On controlled diagnostics and offline MARL benchmarks, MoSDOT improves endpoint quality and routing consistency, particularly on datasets exhibiting multimodal joint behavior.
items.title: Multi-Agent Coordination via Support-Preserving Distillation

Boucenna). All data are synthetic, generated from the exact Mittag-Leffler solution; no experimental or patient data are used.
